blocks.text: The aljarbuo is also said to devise another stratagem. Its windows, or rather its holes, it sometimes covers over with earth at the very surface, so that they may not be visible from outside ^{(10)}. In Arabic this is called دم [damma] damma. Alcamus: دم اليربوع حجره غطاه وسواه [damma al-yarbūʿ juḥrahu ghaṭṭāhu wa-sawwāhu] Damma aljarbuo its hiding place, that is, it covered it and levelled it. Hence the hiding place also has the name دممة [dumama] dumama. The same Alcamus: الدممة حجرة اليربوع وتراب يجمعه اليربوع ويخرجه من الحجر فيسوي به بابه [al-dumama juḥrat al-yarbūʿ wa-turāb yajmaʿuhu al-yarbūʿ wa-yukhrijuhu min al-juḥr fa-yusawwī bihi bābahu] Dumama is the hiding place of the aljarbuo, and the earth which it gathers and digs out of its hiding place in order to level its entrance with it. Accordingly, since the hole of its hiding place, covered with earth, is called نافقا [nāfiqā] naphika, by a metaphor taken from this نافق [nāfaqa] naphaka, a verb of the third conjugation, means to dissemble in religion, and to profess one thing with the mouth while keeping another hidden in the mind. And منافق [munāfiq] munaphik is a hypocrite. Damir: ظاهر بيته تراب وباطنه حفر وكذلك المنافق ظاهره ايمان وباطنه كفر [ẓāhir baytihi turāb wa-bāṭinuhu ḥafr wa-ka-dhālika al-munāfiq ẓāhiruhu īmān wa-bāṭinuhu kufr] The outer part of its house is earth, but the inner part is hollow. Likewise the hypocrite has faith on the outside, but unbelief on the inside. Algiahid and others: واسم المنافق لم يكن في الجاهلية لكن لمن اسر الكفر واظهر الايمان [wa-ism al-munāfiq lam yakun fī al-jāhiliyya lākin li-man asarra al-kufr wa-aẓhara al-īmān] The name munaphik will not be found in heathendom, but (it is said) of him who conceals unbelief and displays faith. Albazi: تعالي اشتق له هذا الاسم من هذا الاصل وهو من نافقا اليربوع لانه لما ابطن الكفر [taʿālā ishtaqqa lahu hādhā al-ism min hādhā al-aṣl wa-huwa min nāfiqā al-yarbūʿ li-annahu lammā abṭana al-kufr] [col. 1013] واظهر الايمان [wa-aẓhara al-īmān] God Most High derived the name of the hypocrite from this root, namely from naphika, or the hole of the mouse called aljarbuo; because within there is unbelief, and without, faith. These and many other things the Arabs say on Azoara 73 of the Qur'an, which is entitled المنافقون [al-munāfiqūn] The Hypocrites. In Alcamus the nest of this animal is called لغز [lughz] [II, 424] logoz, as if you were to say labyrinth, because in nests of this kind the passages are winding and very intricate. And accordingly in Arabic الغاز [alghāz] algaz is the term for طرق تلطوي وتشكل علي مسالكها [ṭuruq talṭawī wa-tushkilu ʿalā masālikihā] paths that are twisted and entangled in their course. To this kind of mouse must be referred what Synesius says of a certain commander John near the end of Epistle 104: Δίκην ἀρουραίου μυὸς ἐνεδεδύκει τῇ πέτρᾳ [dikēn arouraiou myos enededykei tē petra], Like a field mouse he had hidden himself in the rock, that is, in Bombaea, a very strongly fortified stronghold in the hollow of a cliff. For no other field mice nest in rock except the aljarbuo alone ^{(11)}. This is proved by these words of Ibnolgiauzi: اليربوع لا يتخذ بيته الا في موضع صلب مرتفع ليسلم من سيل او حافر ثم لا يجعلة الا عند اكمة او شجرة او صخرة ليلا يضل اذا عاد اليه [al-yarbūʿ lā yattakhidhu baytahu illā fī mawḍiʿ ṣulb murtafiʿ li-yaslama min sayl aw ḥāfir thumma lā yajʿaluhu illā ʿinda akama aw shajara aw ṣakhra li-allā yaḍilla idhā ʿāda ilayhi] The aljarbuo makes its home only in a hard (that is, rocky) and elevated place, so that it may be safe from the inflow of water and from the hoof (of horses). Nor does it set it anywhere but by mounds, or trees, or rocks, lest it go astray when it returns to it. This happens above all to the young of this little animal. Hence the proverb in Damir: اضل من ولد اليربوع [aḍallu min walad al-yarbūʿ] More astray than the young of the aljarbuo, said of one who wanders about and never sets his foot firmly anywhere. In the same place: وفي طباعه انه اذا مشي في ارض سهلة او لينة مشي علي موخر كفه حتي لا يعرف اثر وطيه كما يفعل الارنب [wa-fī ṭibāʿihi annahu idhā mashā fī arḍ sahla aw layyina mashā ʿalā muʾakhkhar kaffihi ḥattā lā yuʿrafa athar waṭʾihi kamā yafʿalu al-arnab] It is also in its nature that, when it walks on soft and yielding ground, it stands on the tips of its feet, so that its tracks may not be recognized in the places it has trodden: which is also the habit of the hare. Likewise: وهو [wa-huwa] [II, 425] يجتر ويبعر وله كرش واسنان واضراس من الفك الاعلي والاسفلي [yajtarru wa-yabʿaru wa-lahu karish wa-asnān wa-aḍrās min al-fakk al-aʿlā wa-al-asfalī] It also ruminates, and voids dung, and has a crop (in the manner of ruminants); although it has teeth and molars both in the upper and in the lower jaw. Peculiar to this same mouse is that it leaps. The Arabs express this by the verb بحظل [baḥẓala] bachdala, which is entirely proper to it. Alcamus: بحظل قفز قفزان اليربوع [baḥẓala qafaza qafazān al-yarbūʿ] Bachdala: he leapt with the leap of the aljarbuo. So also Giauhari. This very thing Theophrastus observed above of those mice that walk on two feet: Ὅταν δὲ διώκωνται, πηδῶσι [hotan de diōkōntai, pēdōsi]· If anyone pursues them, they leap. In its burrows a kind of snake nests, which the Arabs call جنادع [janādiʿ] gianadio, or جنادب [janādib] gianadibo. Alcamus: الجنادع الاجناش اوجنادب تكون في حجرة اليرابيع [al-janādiʿ al-ajnāsh aw janādib takūnu fī juḥrat al-yarābīʿ] Algianadio, (a kind of) serpents, or gianadibo: these are in the nest of the aljarabii [col. 1014], which is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. If the aljarbuo mates with the common mouse, the hybrid mouse born of it is called فرنب [farnab] pharnab, or phirnib. Alcamus: الفرنب الفارة او ولدها من اليربوع [al-farnab al-fāra aw waladuhā min al-yarbūʿ] Alpharnab (or alphirnib) is the mouse, or its offspring by the aljarbuo. This too is peculiar to it, that the aljarbuo is eaten by the Arabs, whereas otherwise the eating of mice is forbidden to them. Damir, in the chapter الفار [al-fār] alphar, that is, On the mouse: يحرم اكل جميع انواع الفار الا اليربوع [yaḥrumu akl jamīʿ anwāʿ al-fār illā al-yarbūʿ] The eating of all species of mouse is forbidden, except the aljarbuo. There is, however, some disagreement among the Arabs on this matter. For according to the opinion of Abuchanipha: لا يوكل لانه من الحشرات [lā yuʾkalu li-annahu min al-ḥasharāt] It (the aljarbuo) is not eaten, because it is one of the subterranean animals. And Algazali, in the book entitled الوسيط [al-Wasīṭ] The Mediator, denies that anything should be eaten من الحشرات الا الضب [min al-ḥasharāt illā al-ḍabb] of the subterranean animals except the land crocodile. Yet others further except اليربوع وابن عرس وام حبين والقنفد والدلدل [al-yarbūʿ wa-ibn ʿirs wa-umm ḥubayn wa-al-qunfud wa-al-duldul] the aljarbuo, and the weasel, and the chameleon, and the hedgehog, and the porcupine. Hence Damir on the aljarbuo: يحل اكله لان العرب تستطيبه وتحله [yaḥillu akluhu li-anna al-ʿArab tastaṭībuhu wa-tuḥilluhu] Its eating is permitted, because the Arabs allow it and delight in it. So indeed the great canonists of the Arabs decide: Ata, and Achmed Ben-Hantal, and Ibnolmandsar, and Abutsaur, etc. Accordingly not only the aljarbuo but also its burrow is bought, that is, the right of searching and probing it so that this animal may be caught in it. Since this, however, usually meets with little success, it has passed into a proverb among the Arabs: as when they say كالمشتري القاصعا باليربوع [ka-al-mushtarī al-qāṣiʿā bi-al-yarbūʿ] Like one who buys, in place of [II, 426] the aljarbuo, its hole. This proverb يضرب الذي يدع العين ويتبع الاثر [yuḍrabu alladhī yadaʿu al-ʿayn wa-yatbaʿu al-athar] is aimed at him who leaves the spring and follows only the track. In Greek you would say Σκιὰν ἀντὶ τοῦ σώματος [skian anti tou sōmatos], The shadow instead of the body. Here too the Arabs are fastidious, and prefer the Supharian to the other mice of this kind, which Alcamus describes thus: يربوع شفاري ضخم الاذنين وطويلهما العاري البراثين ولا يلحق سريعا والطويل والغوايم الرخو اللحم الدسم [yarbūʿ shafārī ḍakhm al-udhunayn wa-ṭawīluhumā al-ʿārī al-barāthīn wa-lā yulḥaqu sarīʿan wa-al-ṭawīl wa-al-ghawāyim al-rikhw al-laḥm al-dasim] The Supharian jarbuo has thick and long ears, is bare of claws, so that it does not easily grip, has long feet, and tender and fat flesh. In Abenbitar: يربوع الاسراييلي لحم اليربوع يقد وغذا كثير ويلين البطن [yarbūʿ al-isrāyīlī laḥm al-yarbūʿ yuqaddu wa-ghadhā kathīr wa-yulayyinu al-baṭn] The Israelite jarbuo is the name for the flesh of the aljarbuo that is dried. It is very nourishing and loosens the bowels. To dry in Arabic is قد [qadda] kadda, which properly [col. 1015] means to expose to the wind meat cut lengthwise, as we do with smoke, so that the moisture may be drawn off. Hence قداد [qaddād] kedad is the name both of the hedgehog and of the aljarbuo, because both animals are dried in this way. Alkamus: القداد القنفد واليربوع [al-qaddād al-qunfud wa-al-yarbūʿ] Alkedado: the hedgehog and the aljarbuo. In the Arabic versions of the Sacred Text the word aljarbuo occurs only once in all, namely at Es. LXVI, 17, where the Arabic translator has: الذين ياكلون لحم الخنازير والرذالات واليربوع [alladhīna yaʾkulūna laḥm al-khanāzīr wa-al-radhālāt wa-al-yarbūʿ] Who eat the flesh of swine, and abominations, and the aljarbua, that is, the species for the genus. For the Hebrew has והעכבר, and the mouse. But the Arab did not lack a reason for rendering it اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbua. For we have already shown that among the Arabs, in the whole genus of mice, this one alone is edible. Moreover, although עכבר achbar means mouse in general for the Hebrews, yet in Arabic this very word عكبر [ʿakbar] achbar, in the plural عكابر [ʿakābir] achabiro, means the male of اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] the aljarbuo. Alcamus: العكابر ذكور من اليرابيع [al-ʿakābir dhukūr min al-yarābīʿ] Alachabiro: the males of the aljarabii, which, as we have already said, is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. Thus, since اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] is the name of the species, العكبر [al-ʿakbar] alachbar denotes the male, as العطيوطة [al-ʿaṭyūṭa] alatiuta denotes the female. Alcamus: العطيوطة اليربوع الانثي [al-ʿaṭyūṭa al-yarbūʿ al-unthā] Alatiuta: the female aljarbuo. The Portuguese Teixeira calls them ratones del mato, that is, mice of the thicket, and describes them in these words in chapter 4 of his Indian Itinerary: Son estos ratones del grandor de los grandes nuestros communes, tienen el pelo pardo tirante à blanco. Tienen de raton las orejas, manos, y la cola: cuya punta, y los ojos, y cabeça, son de conejo; y las piernas como de gazela. Corren mucho saltando, hazen cueua como conejo. Y ay dellos grande quantidad [II, 427] por aquel de sierto. Los Arabes los comen, y dizen, que son muy buenos. That is: These mice are equal in size to the largest of the common ones, and of a whitish-grey colour. They have the ears, forefeet and tail of a mouse; the tip of the tail, the eyes and the head are those of a rabbit; and the haunches (that is, the hind legs) those of a roe deer. They mostly run by leaping, and dig burrows as rabbits do. In that desert (in the part of Arabia bordering on Babylonia) there is a very great abundance of them. The Arabs use them as food, and assert that they are of excellent flavour. In these words the aljarbuo is described in every respect, as no one will deny. Of the same animal Olearius writes thus in book 6 of his Persian Itinerary, page 64: Near Terkin (in Circassia) we saw a kind of field mouse, called in Arabic IERBUA. It has the size of a squirrel, and a form not unlike it; but its fur is darker; and it has the head of a mouse; long ears; the front legs short, the hind legs longer. Hence they run only when going uphill; on level ground they mostly creep, or are carried by a leap above the ground for five or six feet. The tail is long, lying along the back, bare on the stem, hairy and whitish at the tip. It was a pleasant sight to see many of them springing upward at the same moment. They say that Babylonia and Arabia teem with them, and that they serve the inhabitants as food. There are some that come from the fields into houses and steal money.
